It began in the Shah’s showroom: Western reactors, European enrichment deals, Israeli technical cooperation, and the faith that a friendly dictator is just democracy with better catering.

Germany signed reactor contracts. Israel and the Shah’s Iran ran scientific and military cooperation, including the secret Project Flower missile program. Tehran was not a pariah then. It was a client with oil, cash and excellent geopolitical references.

That distinction matters. America and Israel dealt with the Shah’s Iran — a pre-revolutionary ally that they expected to remain manageable. Ukraine’s missiles reached the Islamic Republic decades later, through an illegal export network, not a strategic partnership. Different eras. Different regime. Today’s crypto policy conversation is focused on one question:

Will the CLARITY Act reach a Senate vote before the August recess?

The legislation has already passed an important procedural stage.

On May 14, the Senate Banking Committee advanced the CLARITY Act by a bipartisan 15–9 vote, moving the bill toward consideration by the full Senate.

But Congress is no longer the only institution shaping the market.

The SEC and CFTC have already issued a joint framework that:

• separates digital commodities, stablecoins, digital tools, collectibles and digital securities
• explains how investment-contract rules may apply to crypto transactions
• addresses staking, mining, airdrops and wrapped assets
• begins clarifying the jurisdictional boundary between the two agencies

The SEC’s 2026 regulatory agenda also includes clearer rules for crypto capital formation, custody and trading tokenized securities onchain.

This creates two parallel tracks.

Legislation defines durable authority.

It can determine which regulator oversees which part of the market and create a framework that future administrations cannot easily reverse.

Rulemaking defines practical implementation.

It determines how companies register, how assets are classified, what disclosures are required and how existing law applies today.

The CLARITY Act remains important.

But the market is no longer waiting for one bill to begin changing.

Congress is designing the architecture.
Regulators are already building parts of the operating system.

💬 Lebanon says death toll from Israeli aggression reaches 4,335

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Lebanon’s Health Ministry says the death toll from the latest Israeli aggression against the country has risen to 4,335.

According to a statement by the ministry, carried by Lebanon’s Al Manar news network on Saturday, at least 4,335 people have been killed since the Israeli aggression began on March 2, 2026.
​
The statement put the number of injured at 12,273.
​
Fighting resumed between Israel and Lebanon’s Hezbollah resistance movement in March after the group launched attacks against the regime in response to Israel’s near-daily attacks on Lebanon and the assassination of Iran’s Leader Ayatollah Seyyed Ali Khamenei in a US-Israeli airstrike in Tehran two days earlier.
​
On March 26, Israel launched a ground invasion and subsequently occupied parts of southern Lebanon. On April 16, Israel and Lebanon agreed to a ceasefire, but the truce was repeatedly breached.
​
On June 26, the two sides signed a framework agreement brokered by the United States in Washington. Under the framework, Israeli troops would withdraw from southern Lebanon and be replaced by units of the Lebanese Armed Forces.
​
Hezbollah Secretary General Sheikh Naim Qassem called the framework a surrender to Israel. Critics also pointed to the absence of a specific timetable for the withdrawal of Israeli forces.

🔊 Iran secures historic first gold at global AI olympiad

📌 Tehran, IRNA – Iran’s national team has won its first-ever gold medal at the International Olympiad in Artificial Intelligence (IOAI), securing four medals at the 2026 competition in Astana, Kazakhstan.

The third edition of the IOAI was held from August 2 to 7, bringing together more than 400 participants from over 100 countries. Iran’s young AI researchers delivered a strong performance, winning one gold, two silver and one bronze medal.
​
Shayan Reza-Zadeh claimed the gold medal, while Mohammad-Reza Darvishi and Mohammad-Amin Nazmfar won silver medals. Mani Monjipour secured the team’s bronze medal.
​
The achievement marks a significant milestone for Iran’s participation in the global AI competition and highlights the capabilities of its young researchers in artificial intelligence.
​
The team faced challenges during its preparation, including internet disruptions and damage to national AI infrastructure amid recent acts of aggression by the United States and the Israeli regime. Despite these difficulties, the young researchers maintained their preparations and achieved a historic result at the international competition.
